GENERAL PARTNERSHIP AGREEMENT
Prepared for Morgan & Lee Consulting · Jordan Morgan

FORMATION AND PARTNERS
Morgan & Lee Consulting is a general partnership carrying on business as coowners for profit. Its partners are Jordan Morgan and Casey Lee.

FORMATION — WITH OR WITHOUT A WRITTEN AGREEMENT
California's partnership statute treats Morgan & Lee Consulting as formed by law itself, not by this or any other document: the association of two or more persons — here, Jordan Morgan and Casey Lee — to carry on as coowners a business for profit forms a partnership, whether or not those persons intend to form one. The statute separately defines a "partnership agreement" as the agreement among partners concerning the partnership, which can be written, oral, or implied — meaning a general partnership, unlike the corporations and LLCs this project also documents, can exist under California law with no signed paperwork at all. This document memorializes and supplements whatever partnership already exists (or is being formed) between the parties named above.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Partnership” means an association of two or more persons to carry on as coowners a business for profit formed under Section 16202, predecessor law, or comparable law of another jurisdiction, and includes, for all purposes of the laws of this state, a registered limited liability partnership, and excludes any partnership formed under Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 15900)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16101(a)(9), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, statutory definition of 'partnership' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=5.&article=1.)
  "“Partnership agreement” means the agreement, whether written, oral, or implied, among the partners concerning the partnership, including amendments to the partnership agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16101(a)(10), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, a 'partnership agreement' can be written, oral, or implied (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=5.&article=1.)
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (b), the association of two or more persons to carry on as coowners a business for profit forms a partnership, whether or not the persons intend to form a partnership."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16202(a), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, formation by operation of law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16202.)
  "(b) An association formed under a statute other than this chapter, a predecessor statute, or a comparable statute of another jurisdiction is not a partnership under this chapter."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16202(b), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, exception for associations formed under another statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16202.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how general partnership formation works as a matter of law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. The formation rule quoted above has real, narrower statutory carve-outs beyond the ones quoted here: an association formed under a different statute (Corp. Code § 16202(b)) is not a partnership under this chapter, and separate provisions of the same section state that joint tenancy, tenancy in common, and similar co-ownership arrangements do not by themselves establish a partnership, and that receiving a share of profits as payment of a debt, wages, rent, an annuity, loan interest, or the sale price of business goodwill does not by itself make the recipient a partner (Corp. Code § 16202(c)). Two of these four citations (§ 16101(a)(9) and § 16101(a)(10)) are subsections of the same statutory section; no additional independent source was found for that specific point beyond it.

CAPITAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Morgan & Lee Consulting has received the following initial capital contributions from its partners:

Jordan Morgan: $25,000 cash
Casey Lee: $25,000 cash

SHARING PROFITS AND LOSSES — THE DEFAULT RULE
Absent a different rule stated in this agreement, California partnership law entitles each partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting to an equal share of partnership profits, and makes each partner chargeable with a share of partnership losses in proportion to that partner's share of the profits — regardless of how much capital, property, or work each partner actually contributed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) Each partner is entitled to an equal share of the partnership profits and, subject to Sections 16306 and 16957, is chargeable with a share of the partnership losses in proportion to the partner’s share of the profits."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16401(b), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, default equal profit share and proportional loss share (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16401.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, often-surprising default profit-and-loss allocation rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Nothing about this default is affected by unequal capital contributions: two partners who contributed vastly different amounts of capital still split profits equally under this rule unless their partnership agreement (which, as noted elsewhere in this document, doesn't have to be written) sets a different split. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 16401(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

MANAGEMENT RIGHTS — THE DEFAULT RULE
Absent a different rule stated in this agreement, California partnership law gives each partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting equal rights in the management and conduct of the partnership's business — regardless of each partner's capital contribution, time commitment, or role.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(f) Each partner has equal rights in the management and conduct of the partnership business."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16401(f), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, default equal management rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16401.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the default management rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. The same statutory section separately defaults ordinary-course business decisions to majority-of-partners approval, and reserves acts outside the ordinary course of business, and any amendment to the partnership agreement, for unanimous consent — defaults this document's own management and voting terms may or may not track. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 16401(f)); no additional independent source was found for this.

PARTNERS' FIDUCIARY DUTIES TO EACH OTHER
Each partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting owes the partnership and the other partners a duty of loyalty and a duty of care. The duty of loyalty requires a partner to account for and hold as trustee any property, profit, or benefit the partner derives from the partnership's business or from using partnership property or information (including taking a partnership opportunity for themselves); to refrain from dealing with the partnership on behalf of someone whose interests are adverse to it; and to refrain from competing with the partnership before it dissolves. The duty of care is narrower than it might sound: it's limited to refraining from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law — ordinary negligence, by itself, does not breach it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) The fiduciary duties a partner owes to the partnership and the other partners are the duty of loyalty and the duty of care set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16404(a), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the two fiduciary duties a partner owes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16404.)
  "(b) A partner’s duty of loyalty to the partnership and the other partners includes all of the following: (1) To account to the partnership and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the partner in the conduct and winding up of the partnership business or derived from a use by the partner of partnership property or information, including the appropriation of a partnership opportunity. (2) To refrain from dealing with the partnership in the conduct or winding up of the partnership business as or on behalf of a party having an interest adverse to the partnership. (3) To refrain from competing with the partnership in the conduct of the partnership business before the dissolution of the partnership."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16404(b), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the statutory duty of loyalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16404.)
  "(c) A partner’s duty of care to the partnership and the other partners in the conduct and winding up of the partnership business is limited to refraining from engaging in grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16404(c), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the statutory duty of care — a low bar, not ordinary negligence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16404.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default fiduciary-duty structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Every partner also owes an independent obligation of good faith and fair dealing in exercising rights and discharging duties, and a partner does not violate any of these duties merely by acting in their own self-interest — the statute states both points directly. All three citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16404); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

PARTNERSHIP PROPERTY VS. A PARTNER'S OWN PROPERTY
Whether an asset counts as Morgan & Lee Consulting's property, or as one partner's own separate property, turns on a specific statutory test rather than on whoever happens to be using it. Property is partnership property if it's acquired in the partnership's own name, or acquired by one or more partners with the instrument transferring title indicating either their capacity as partners or the partnership's existence — and property is presumed to be partnership property if it was purchased with partnership assets, even without such an indication. Conversely, property acquired in a partner's own name, with no indication of partnership capacity or existence and without using partnership assets, is presumed to be that partner's separate property — even if the partnership actually uses it for partnership purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Property is partnership property if acquired in the name of either of the following: (1) The partnership. (2) One or more partners with an indication in the instrument transferring title to the property of the person’s capacity as a partner or of the existence of a partnership but without an indication of the name of the partnership. (b) Property is acquired in the name of the partnership by a transfer to either of the following: (1) The partnership in its name. (2) One or more partners in their capacity as partners in the partnership, if the name of the partnership is indicated in the instrument transferring title to the property. (c) Property is presumed to be partnership property if purchased with partnership assets, even if not acquired in the name of the partnership or of one or more partners with an indication in the instrument transferring title to the property of the person’s capacity as a partner or of the existence of a partnership."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16204(a)-(c), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the test for partnership property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16204.)
  "(d) Property acquired in the name of one or more of the partners, without an indication in the instrument transferring title to the property of the person’s capacity as a partner or of the existence of a partnership and without use of partnership assets, is presumed to be separate property, even if used for partnership purposes."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16204(d), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the presumption of separate (non-partnership) property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16204.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory ownership test — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Both directions of this test are rebuttable presumptions, not absolute rules — the statute itself frames the partnership-assets presumption and the partner's-own-name presumption as presumptions, not conclusive determinations. Both citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16204); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

EACH PARTNER'S PERSONAL LIABILITY FOR PARTNERSHIP OBLIGATIONS
California partnership law does not give Morgan & Lee Consulting's partners the liability shield that the LLCs and corporations covered elsewhere in this project have: all partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the partnership, unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law. A partner admitted into an already-existing partnership is not personally liable for a partnership obligation that was incurred before that partner was admitted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), all partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the partnership unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(a), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, joint and several liability for partnership obligations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16306.)
  "(b) A person admitted as a partner into an existing partnership is not personally liable for any partnership obligation incurred before the person’s admission as a partner."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(b), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, a newly admitted partner isn't liable for pre-admission obligations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16306.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a general partnership's default liability structure has no shield comparable to an LLC's or corporation's — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. The statute carves out a distinct, separate liability regime for a "registered limited liability partnership" (Corp. Code § 16306(c)-(h)), a different, specifically-registered entity type that this document does not cover. Both citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16306); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

PARTNER'S RIGHT TO PARTNERSHIP BOOKS AND RECORDS
Partners of Morgan & Lee Consulting have a statutory right to access the partnership's books and records: the partnership must provide partners (and their agents and attorneys) access to inspect and copy its books and records during ordinary business hours, and a former partner retains that same access for the period during which they were a partner. The partnership may charge a reasonable fee, covering the cost of labor and materials, for copies it furnishes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) A partnership shall provide partners and their agents and attorneys access to its books and records. It shall provide former partners and their agents and attorneys access to books and records pertaining to the period during which they were partners. The right of access provides the opportunity to inspect and copy books and records during ordinary business hours. A partnership may impose a reasonable charge, covering the costs of labor and material, for copies of documents furnished."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16403(b), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, partner and former-partner access to books and records (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16403.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine partner records-access right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 16403(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

DISSOCIATION — WHAT TRIGGERS A PARTNER LEAVING THE PARTNERSHIP
A partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting is legally "dissociated" from the partnership — meaning that partner's status as a partner ends — on the occurrence of any of several specific statutory events: the partnership's having notice of that partner's express will to withdraw (or a later withdrawal date the partner specifies); an event the partnership agreement itself designates as causing dissociation; the partner's expulsion under the partnership agreement's own terms, by unanimous vote of the other partners under specific statutory circumstances, or by judicial determination; the partner becoming a debtor in bankruptcy or a similar insolvency event occurring; and, for a partner who is an individual, that partner's death, incapacity, or the appointment of a guardian or conservator for them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A partner is dissociated from a partnership upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) The partnership’s having notice of the partner’s express will to withdraw as a partner or on a later date specified by the partner."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(1), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation by a partner's express will to withdraw (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16601.)
  "(2) An event agreed to in the partnership agreement as causing the partner’s dissociation. (3) The partner’s expulsion pursuant to the partnership agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(2)-(3), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation by agreed event or agreement-based expulsion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16601.)
  "(6) The partner’s act or failure to act in any of the following instances: (A) By becoming a debtor in bankruptcy."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(6)(A), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation on becoming a debtor in bankruptcy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16601.)
  "(7) In the case of a partner who is an individual, by any of the following: (A) The partner’s death. (B) The appointment of a guardian or general conservator for the partner. (C) A judicial determination that the partner has otherwise become incapable of performing the partner’s duties under the partnership agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(7), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation of an individual partner by death or incapacity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16601.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory list of dissociation triggers — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Dissociation is a distinct legal event from dissolution of the entire partnership; a companion clause in this document addresses when dissociation does, and does not, trigger dissolution. The statute lists additional dissociation events, for partners that are corporate entities, trusts, or estates, that this summary does not itemize. All citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16601); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

DISSOLUTION — A PARTNER'S DEPARTURE DOESN'T ALWAYS END THE PARTNERSHIP
Under California's current partnership statute, a partner's dissociation from Morgan & Lee Consulting does not, by itself, automatically dissolve the partnership. Instead, the partnership dissolves only on the occurrence of specific listed events. If Morgan & Lee Consulting is a partnership at will (the partners haven't agreed to a fixed term or a particular undertaking), dissolution requires the express will to wind up the business from at least half of the partners, including any partners who wrongfully dissociated within the preceding 90 days. If Morgan & Lee Consulting instead has a definite term or a particular undertaking, dissolution can be triggered after certain kinds of partner dissociation (such as death) if a majority in interest of the remaining partners doesn't agree to continue the partnership within 90 days, by the express will of all partners to wind up the business, or by the expiration of the term or completion of the undertaking. Other listed events — an event the partnership agreement itself designates, an uncured illegality, or specific judicial determinations — can also trigger dissolution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A partnership is dissolved, and its business shall be wound up, only upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) In a partnership at will, by the express will to dissolve and wind up the partnership business of at least half of the partners, including partners, other than wrongfully dissociating partners, who have dissociated within the preceding 90 days, and for which purpose a dissociation under paragraph (1) of Section 16601 constitutes an expression of that partner’s will to dissolve and wind up the partnership business."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(1), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution trigger for an at-will partnership (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16801.)
  "(2) In a partnership for a definite term or particular undertaking, when any of the following occurs: (A) After the expiration of 90 days after a partner’s dissociation by death or otherwise under paragraphs (6) to (10), inclusive, of Section 16601, or a partner’s wrongful dissociation under subdivision (b) of Section 16602 unless before that time a majority in interest of the partners, including partners who have rightfully dissociated pursuant to subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 16602, agree to continue the partnership."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(2)(A), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution trigger for a term partnership after certain dissociations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16801.)
  "(B) The express will of all of the partners to wind up the partnership business. (C) The expiration of the term or the completion of the undertaking."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(2)(B)-(C), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution of a term partnership by unanimous will or term expiration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16801.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's modern partnership law does not automatically dissolve a partnership every time a partner leaves — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership, and not a claim about how any particular older or other state's partnership statute treats dissociation. This is a genuinely significant change from the 1914 Uniform Partnership Act's default rule, under which most partner departures did dissolve the partnership by operation of law; California adopted the newer Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 (RUPA-based) framework quoted here, which decouples a partner's exit from the partnership's continued existence in most circumstances. All citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16801); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Adopted and agreed to by all partners:

☐ _________________________ Jordan Morgan   Date: _______________

☐ _________________________ Casey Lee   Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: Under California's current partnership statute, a partner's dissociation from Morgan & Lee Consulting does not, by itself, automatically dissolve the partnership. Instead, the partnership dissolves only on the occurrence of specific listed events. If Morgan & Lee Consulting is a partnership at will (the partners haven't agreed to a fixed term or a particular undertaking), dissolution requires the express will to wind up the business from at least half of the partners, including any partners who wrongfully dissociated within the preceding 90 days. If Morgan & Lee Consulting instead has a definite term or a particular undertaking, dissolution can be triggered after certain kinds of partner dissociation (such as death) if a majority in interest of the remaining partners doesn't agree to continue the partnership within 90 days, by the express will of all partners to wind up the business, or by the expiration of the term or completion of the undertaking. Other listed events — an event the partnership agreement itself designates, an uncured illegality, or specific judicial determinations — can also trigger dissolution.

citations.quote: (2) In a partnership for a definite term or particular undertaking, when any of the following occurs: (A) After the expiration of 90 days after a partner’s dissociation by death or otherwise under paragraphs (6) to (10), inclusive, of Section 16601, or a partner’s wrongful dissociation under subdivision (b) of Section 16602 unless before that time a majority in interest of the partners, including partners who have rightfully dissociated pursuant to subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 16602, agree to continue the partnership.
